opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing I'd say is that governance can't be just a set of principles on a wall. Most organizations already agree on the principles: fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, transparency, accountability. The hard part is turning those into something people actually do day to day.

Practically, I think about it in a few layers.

The first is **clear policy and requirements**. You need a standard that tells teams concretely what's expected. Not "be fair," but "for this kind of system, you need to identify the stakeholders who could be affected, assess these specific harms, and meet these bars before you ship." If the requirement isn't actionable, it won't get implemented consistently.

The second is **process and checkpoints**. Governance has to show up at the right moments in the development lifecycle. That means an impact assessment early, while you can still change the design, and a review before release. It also means a path for escalating the sensitive or high-risk cases to people with deeper expertise. Not everything needs the same level of scrutiny, so a risk-based triage is really important. Otherwise you either slow everything down or rubber-stamp everything.

The third, and I think the one people underestimate, is **tooling**. You can't ask every engineering team to become experts in measuring jailbreak susceptibility, groundedness, or harmful content. If you want people to do the right thing, you have to make it the easy thing. That means shared evaluation tools, red-teaming practices, content filters and other mitigations, and monitoring they can plug in, rather than every team reinventing it. This has become even more critical with generative AI, because the risk surface is so broad and changes so quickly.

The fourth is **people and culture**. You need clear accountability, meaning someone who owns the outcome for each system. You also need a network of people embedded in product teams who understand responsible AI and can translate between policy and engineering. Training matters, but so does leadership signaling that this is part of shipping a quality product, not a tax on it.

And finally, **governance has to be iterative**. The technology is moving fast, regulations are evolving, and you'll learn things in deployment you didn't anticipate. So you need feedback loops: incident response, monitoring in production, and a way to update your requirements and tools based on what you learn.

If I had to boil it down, I'd say: make the requirements concrete, build them into the workflow, and invest heavily in tools so teams can actually meet them. That's what turns governance from a document into practice.

r001.rationale: The response lists principles such as privacy, fairness, and security and mentions assessing harms, but it does not clearly identify governance risk decisions as extending beyond safety risks.

r002.rationale: It discusses accountability and leadership support, but does not recommend a leadership-level committee to decide which AI risks the organization will accept.

r003.rationale: It recommends a pre-release review and escalation of high-risk cases to people with deeper expertise, but does not make release contingent on expert review of readiness against the assessed risks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks so much for having me, Sam. It's great to be here.

So I think the first thing I'd say is that governance is not a document. I think a lot of organizations start by writing principles, and principles are important, but they're the easy part. Almost everybody agrees on fairness, reliability, privacy, transparency. The hard part is operationalizing those principles so that they actually change what gets built and shipped. So when I think about what's practical, I think about a few things.

The first is that you need a process that's integrated into how people already work. If responsible AI is a separate checklist that lands on someone's desk two weeks before launch, it's going to fail, or it's going to be a rubber stamp. What we found is that it has to be woven into the development lifecycle, so you're identifying potential harms when you're scoping the system, you're measuring them as you build, you're mitigating, and then you're monitoring once it's in production. That loop of identify, measure, mitigate, operate is really the backbone.

The second piece is that you need the right people with the right expertise, and you need clear accountability. Who owns the risk for a given system? In a lot of organizations, that question doesn't have an answer, and when nobody owns it, it doesn't get managed. You also want a mix of perspectives, so engineers and data scientists, but also people who understand policy, legal, the domain, and ideally the communities that are going to be affected. Those sociotechnical questions can't be answered by one discipline.

The third thing, and this is the one I'm most passionate about, is measurement and tooling. If you can't measure a harm, it's very hard to govern it. So investing in evaluation, in red teaming, in being able to systematically test a system for things like groundedness or harmful content or disparities across groups, that turns governance from a judgment call into something you can actually track and improve. And with generative AI especially, the failure modes are so open-ended that you really need a layered approach, so safety in the model, safety in the system around it, and monitoring in production, because you will not catch everything up front.

And then the last thing I'd say is that you have to accept that you're going to learn as you go. The technology is moving incredibly fast, and the governance has to be adaptive. The organizations that do this well treat it as something they iterate on, where every incident or near miss feeds back into the process, rather than something they finish and put on a shelf.

r001.rationale: The response discusses fairness, privacy, disparities, and other governance concerns, but does not clearly say that governance risk decisions extend beyond safety risks.

r002.rationale: It calls for clear accountability and the right mix of expertise, but does not recommend a leadership-level committee to decide which risks the organization will accept.

r003.rationale: It recommends integrating governance into development and measuring risks, but does not make release contingent on expert review of readiness against assessed risks.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important thing is translating principles into decisions people can actually make. You can have a commitment to fairness, privacy, or transparency, but a team building a system needs to understand what that means for their particular use case. Who could be affected? What could go wrong? What evidence do we need before we’re comfortable deploying it?

Then you need clear ownership. Who is responsible for assessing those risks, who can help the team address them, and who makes the call when there’s a difficult tradeoff? That takes collaboration across engineering, product, legal, and policy, as well as people who understand the context in which the system will be used.

And you need to make that process part of how teams already build products. Give them practical tools, guidance, and access to expertise early, when they can still change the design. If governance only shows up as a review at the very end, it’s much harder to be effective.

Finally, it can’t stop at deployment. You need monitoring, feedback, and a way to respond when the system behaves differently than you expected. Governance should help an organization learn and improve as it uses AI.

r001.rationale: It identifies risks tied to fairness, privacy, and transparency, alongside what could go wrong for affected people, so governance decisions extend beyond safety alone.

r002.rationale: It discusses ownership and who makes difficult tradeoffs, but does not recommend a leadership-level committee to decide which risks the organization will accept.

r003.rationale: It asks what evidence is needed before deployment and mentions late-stage review, but does not recommend making release contingent on expert readiness review against assessed risks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important thing is translating principles into decisions people can actually make. It’s relatively easy to say, “We care about fairness, privacy, and transparency.” The harder question is: What does that mean for the team building a particular application, and who is accountable for making sure those concerns are addressed?

Practically, I’d start with understanding where AI is being used and what the risks are in each context. A tool that helps someone draft a document needs a different level of oversight from a system that influences access to a consequential service. You need a process for assessing those risks early, while there’s still an opportunity to change the design.

Then you need to give teams concrete support: clear requirements, evaluation tools, documentation, and a way to bring difficult questions to people with the right expertise. Governance works much better when it’s integrated into the development process and supported by engineering, legal, policy, and domain experts.

And it has to continue after deployment. You need monitoring, feedback, and a way to respond when something goes wrong. For me, the practical test is whether governance helps a team recognize an issue, make a better decision, and know when to ask for help.

r001.rationale: It discusses assessing risks by context and oversight, but does not clearly identify governance decisions as extending beyond safety risks.

r002.rationale: It recommends bringing difficult questions to people with relevant expertise, but does not call for a leadership-level committee to decide which risks the organization will accept.

r003.rationale: It recommends early risk assessment and ongoing monitoring, but does not make release contingent on expert review of readiness against the assessed risks.
